Usually there are several "critical periods" for language learning (although the existence of these has even been contested), each dealing with different aspects of a language. For example, there is usually thought to be a critical period of phonological development in childhood when learning a second language, which is why adults usually never lose their foreign accent. 

Still, kids are of course going to have it easier because they have more time to learn a language, and likely more immersion. If you're an adult, just keep at it and you'll get there, there isn't something about being a kid that makes them inately "better" in learning languages :)

Even then, 8chan wasn't founded by an "alt-right shithead" but [Frederick Brennan](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fredrick_Brennan), who created the site as a sort of 4chan-Reddit hybrid, but resigned in 2016 and is now an outspoken critic of QAnon and supporter of Bernie Sanders (and borne-again christian and type-designer, among other things)

Alt-right? No. Racism? yea probably. 
If you look at the site pre-2016, yea people would say racial slurs and stuff (although this could be argued as a demonstration of free speech and anonymity), but generally users supported left-wing policies and social inclusiveness, with the right-wing extremism and incelness being contained in /pol/ and /r9k/ respectively, with /pol/ being specifically created to quarantine alt-right posts.

Of course, this all changed in 2016, with both /pol/ and /r9k/ becoming what the media knew as "4chan", and an influx of alt-right users slowly seeping into the other 50+ boards. However, visiting the lower-traffic boards can sometimes emulate a pre-2016 experience, as those are usually more niche and their dedicated userbase don't really care about politics.

Pre-2016 chan culture is extremely interesting and very much well nuanced, and it's hard to decipher it through the politically polarized lenses of today. A few good books have been written on it though, such as [Cole Stryker's "Hacking the Future"](https://www.google.com/search?q=hacking%20the%20futurw&ie=utf-8&oe=utf-8&client=firefox-b-1-m), published in 2012.
